Investigation journey from source checkpoints:

OPP-011-01.md: The strongest current conclusion is:

> **Medication reconciliation discrepancies are directly documented at Fortis Hospital Mohali and independently documented across multiple Indian hospitals. This is a high-consequence, repeatable healthcare workflow involving clinical investigation and discrepancy resolution. The remaining unknown is whether sufficient unresolved human coordination exists beyond existing hospital systems to create an ART automation opportunity.**

**OPP-011-01 = PASS → CONTINUE**

**Next: OPP-011-02 — Exception + Human Investigation Reconstruction**

OPP-011-02.md: The evidence supports a strong conclusion:

> **Medication discrepancies create a high-consequence exception workflow requiring information recovery, authorised clinical clarification, follow-up, documentation and closure. Fortis Mohali is directly represented in Indian evidence showing substantial discrepancy burden, and similar workflows are documented across other hospitals.**

The unresolved question is no longer whether the workflow exists.

It is:

> **How much residual human investigation and unresolved coordination remains after the hospital's existing systems?**

**OPP-011-02 = PASS → CONTINUE**

**Next: OPP-011-03 — Human Effort / Pain Quantification**

OPP-011-03.md: The strongest defensible conclusion is:

> **Medication reconciliation can require substantial human effort, and Fortis Mohali has directly documented a substantial discrepancy burden. External time-and-motion evidence shows that medication reconciliation, discrepancy investigation and discharge coordination can consume meaningful staff time. The strongest ART opportunity is not generic reconciliation automation; it is preventing identified, time-sensitive discrepancies from remaining unresolved through ownership, follow-up and escalation.**

**OPP-011-03 = PASS → HIGH-EFFORT / HIGH-CONSEQUENCE OPPORTUNITY SIGNAL**

**Next: OPP-011-04 — Direct Operational Evidence / Pain Validation**

OPP-011-04.md: The strongest defensible conclusion is:

> **Fortis Mohali provides unusually strong company-linked evidence of medication-discrepancy and medication-safety activity. However, public research does not reveal whether its current systems already close the discrepancy loop or whether substantial human follow-up remains.**

Therefore **OPP-011 is not yet commercially validated**.

**OPP-011-04 = CONDITIONAL PASS → PRIMARY VALIDATION JUSTIFIED**

The investigation should now pause here for **primary operational validation** rather than adding another desk-research checkpoint.

### E-001 — Company-Specific Primary Research

[PubMed — Medication Reconciliation and Patient Safety in India](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41419375/)

**Evidence:** Fortis Hospital Mohali and Fortis Hospital Ludhiana; 200 inpatients; medication reconciliation at admission, transition and discharge; 170 admission discrepancies, 23 transition discrepancies and 266 discharge discrepancies.

### E-002 — Full Journal Source

[Joint Commission Journal on Quality and Patient Safety — 2026 Study](https://www.jointcommissionjournal.com/article/S1553-7250%2825%2900311-3/pdf)

**Evidence:** detailed study abstract and Fortis affiliations.

### E-003 — Indian Systematic Review

[Indian Journal of Critical Care Medicine — Medication Errors in Indian Hospitals](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12683552/)

**Evidence:** 40 Indian hospital studies; medication-error incidence/frequency and severity.

### E-004 — Emergency / Admission Reconciliation

[PubMed — Shree Krishna Hospital Study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39539902/)

**Evidence:** 64 discrepancies among 45 patients; 25 unintentional omission discrepancies; moderate/severe discrepancies.

### E-005 — Care-Transition Study

[ScienceDirect — Medication Discrepancies Across Transitions](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S2772953222000296)

**Evidence:** 105 unintentional discrepancies among 165 patients with substantial discrepancy occurrence at ICU-to-ward transition and discharge.

### E-006 — Discharge Reconciliation

[Indian Journal of Pharmacy Practice — Discharge Medication Reconciliation](https://www.ijopp.org/article/18/1/53)

**Evidence:** 255 patients; 412 discrepancies; 191 unintentional; omission and dose changes prominent.

---

### E-001 — Fortis Mohali / Ludhiana Study

[PubMed — Medication Reconciliation and Patient Safety in India](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41419375/)

**Evidence:** 200 inpatients; admission, transition and discharge reconciliation; discrepancies documented at all three stages; Fortis Mohali and Ludhiana affiliations.

### E-002 — Medication-Reconciliation Workflow

[PMC — Transition of Care Team](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5922563/)

**Evidence:** medication information gathered from multiple sources; discrepancies investigated; clinician verification; ownership/coordination problems; follow-up.

### E-003 — Documentation / Communication

[PMC — Real-Time Medication Change Documentation](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11214548/)

**Evidence:** incomplete documentation associated with discharge discrepancy errors; real-time documentation improved physician-pharmacist communication.

### E-004 — Indian Discharge Evidence

[Indian Journal of Pharmacy Practice — Discharge Medication Reconciliation](https://www.ijopp.org/article/18/1/53)

**Evidence:** 255 patients; 412 discrepancies; 191 unintentional discrepancies.

### E-005 — Responsibility / Ownership

[PMC — Who Is Responsible for Medication Reconciliation?](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5310138/)

**Evidence:** different perceptions among pharmacists, physicians and nurses regarding responsibility for medication-reconciliation tasks.

### E-006 — Cross-Sector Exception Resolution

[PMC — Cross-Sectoral Hospital Pharmacist Intervention](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10026123/)

**Evidence:** medication-related problems during transitions required medication review, record access and follow-up; intervention identified and solved drug-related problems.

---

### E-001 — Fortis Mohali / Ludhiana Direct Study

[PubMed — Medication Reconciliation and Patient Safety in India](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41419375/)

**Evidence:** 200 inpatients; 170 admission discrepancies; 23 transition discrepancies; 266 discharge discrepancies; discharge highest discrepancy rate per patient.

[PMC — Medication Reconciliation at Hospital Admission](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8446815/)

[PMC — Pharmacist Discharge Medicine Lists](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9243950/)

[PMC — Pharmacist–Doctor Collaborative Discharge Reconciliation](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13369220/)

**Evidence:** reconciliation completion reduced 76→30 minutes; discharge departure reduced 78 minutes; 27% of pharmacist plans required physician adjustment.

### E-005 — Discharge Reconciliation Workload

[PMC — Medication Reconciliation at Admission and Discharge](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3842651/)

**Evidence:** discharge reconciliation time varied by unit and could approach 29 minutes in geriatrics.

### E-006 — Harm / Workload Improvement

[PMC — Improving Medication Reconciliation Accuracy](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6683109/)

**Evidence:** systematic discharge reconciliation reduced pharmacy workload and reported reductions of up to 40 minutes per patient in pharmacy time.

### E-007 — Pharmacist Intervention

[PMC — Pharmacist-Led Medication Reconciliation Meta-analysis](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5873985/)

**Evidence:** pharmacist-led interventions reduced medication discrepancies; effects on adverse drug events/healthcare utilisation were less certain.

The emerging industry-level problem is:

> **Medication discrepancies are identified during care transitions, but resolution requires authorised humans to investigate, clarify, reconcile, document and close exceptions across clinical roles and systems.**

Potential target population:

```text
MID-SCALE / MULTISPECIALITY HOSPITALS
        +
INPATIENT CARE
        +
PHARMACY / MEDICATION MANAGEMENT
        +
ADMISSION / TRANSFER / DISCHARGE
        +
MEDICATION RECONCILIATION
```

The opportunity is therefore potentially reusable across many Indian hospitals.


### High


### Screening range

> **≈50–600 hypothetical exception-hours/year**

This is **not Fortis actual workload**.

---

The labour-only model gives:

> **Base: ~200 hours/year**

At ₹750/hour:

> **~₹1.5 lakh/year labour-value exposure**

At a hypothetical 50% capture:

> **~₹75,000/year addressable labour value**

That is still not a large standalone SaaS opportunity.

Therefore the commercial case should be:

```text
LABOUR VALUE
+
TRANSITION DELAY REDUCTION
+
UNRESOLVED-CASE REDUCTION
+
AUDIT / QUALITY VISIBILITY
+
PATIENT-SAFETY RISK REDUCTION
```

But only the first component can currently be numerically hypothesised.

---

The previous checkpoint used hypothetical values such as:

```text
50–200 discrepancies/month
5–15 minutes/exception
```

Those were explicitly labelled assumptions.

They **must not be presented as Fortis operational data**.

The current evidence is strong enough to justify primary validation, but not strong enough to calculate Fortis ROI.

**Industry:** Healthcare / Hospital Operations  
**Company:** Fortis Hospital Mohali  
**Workflow:** Medication Reconciliation Exception Resolution at Care Transitions  
**Pain type:** Patient Safety / Medication Discrepancy Resolution  
**VRL checkpoint:** OPP-011-01  
**Decision:** **PASS → High-consequence workflow target**

---

This investigation deliberately moves away from low-value administrative automation.

The target is:

> **Medication discrepancy discovered during admission, transfer or discharge → investigation → clarification → resolution → documented closure.**

This is a **patient-safety workflow**, not merely a productivity workflow.

A 2026 prospective Indian study conducted at Fortis Hospital Mohali and Fortis Hospital Ludhiana found medication discrepancies at admission, transition and discharge, with the highest discrepancy rate per patient occurring at discharge.

---

These are **study observations at Fortis Hospital Mohali/Ludhiana**, not necessarily current hospital-wide operating metrics.

The evidence is nevertheless unusually strong for VRL because the target company itself appears in the primary research population.

---

The underlying workflow is:

```text
PATIENT ARRIVES / TRANSFERS / PREPARES FOR DISCHARGE
                 ↓
COLLECT CURRENT MEDICATION INFORMATION
                 ↓
COMPARE:
- PATIENT-REPORTED MEDICATIONS
- PREVIOUS RECORDS
- CURRENT ORDERS
- DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS
                 ↓
IDENTIFY DISCREPANCIES
                 ↓
CLASSIFY
                 ↓
CLINICIAN / PHARMACIST REVIEW
                 ↓
RESOLVE
                 ↓
DOCUMENT
                 ↓
CLOSE
```

Medication reconciliation is specifically intended to identify and prevent medication errors and discrepancies during transitions of care.

---

The important workflow is not the routine reconciliation.

It is:

```text
MEDICATION LISTS DO NOT MATCH
             ↓
WHICH MEDICATION IS CORRECT?
             ↓
WHY DOES THE DIFFERENCE EXIST?
             ↓
IS IT INTENTIONAL?
             ↓
WHO MUST CONFIRM?
             ↓
CLINICIAN / PHARMACIST INVESTIGATION
             ↓
CORRECTION / CONFIRMATION
             ↓
DOCUMENT
             ↓
CLOSE
```

This creates a genuine **human investigation loop**.

---

At Fortis Mohali/Ludhiana, the 2026 study recorded:

```text
ADMISSION
170 discrepancies

TRANSITION
23 discrepancies

DISCHARGE
266 discrepancies
```

The discharge phase produced the highest discrepancy burden per patient.

This is much stronger evidence than merely finding that “medication reconciliation is recommended.”

---

Medication errors are among the most common preventable patient-safety errors.

A 2025 systematic review of **40 Indian hospital studies** found a median medication-error incidence of **34.11%** across 10 studies and a medication-error frequency rate of **26.74%** across 28 studies. The review also reported that some medication errors caused temporary harm or prolonged hospitalization.

This does **not** mean Fortis has those rates.

It demonstrates that medication discrepancies/errors are a serious, recurring Indian hospital safety problem.

---

This is particularly valuable for ART because the same workflow has been independently observed in multiple Indian hospital settings.

A study at Shree Krishna Hospital in Gujarat found **64 medication discrepancies among 45 emergency/trauma patients**, including **25 unintentional omission discrepancies**, with many classified as moderate to severe.

Another Indian study of care transitions found **105 unintentional discrepancies among 165 patients with 159 total discrepancies**, with substantial discrepancy occurrence during ICU-to-ward transition and discharge.

A 2024 Indian discharge study involving **255 patients** found **412 medication discrepancies**, of which **191 were unintentional**; drug omission and altered dose were major categories.

Therefore:

> **The same underlying exception pattern appears across multiple Indian hospital settings.**

That is the beginning of an **industry-level opportunity**, not merely a Fortis opportunity.

---

ART should not prescribe or decide medication changes.

The potential automation layer is:

```text
DISCREPANCY DETECTED
        ↓
CREATE EXCEPTION
        ↓
CLASSIFY
        ↓
ASSIGN RESPONSIBLE OWNER
        ↓
REQUEST CLARIFICATION
        ↓
TRACK RESPONSE
        ↓
AGE
        ↓
ESCALATE
        ↓
CONFIRM RESOLUTION
        ↓
AUDIT TRAIL
```

ART's role:

> **Make unresolved medication discrepancies visible, owned, aged and escalated until an authorised clinical decision closes them.**

Clinical decision remains with the authorised clinician/pharmacist.

---

The evidence-supported workflow is:

```text
PATIENT ENTERS / TRANSFERS / DISCHARGES
              ↓
OBTAIN BEST POSSIBLE MEDICATION HISTORY
              ↓
COMPARE WITH CURRENT ORDERS / DISCHARGE PLAN
              ↓
IDENTIFY DIFFERENCES
              ↓
DETERMINE:
INTENTIONAL OR UNINTENTIONAL?
              ↓
CLINICAL REVIEW
              ↓
RESOLVE
              ↓
DOCUMENT
              ↓
CLOSE
```

A published medication-reconciliation implementation describes comparison of medication history against current orders, identification of discrepancies, discussion with the prescribing physician and resolution.

---

The first major exception is:

```text
HISTORICAL MEDICATION
        ≠
CURRENT ORDER
```

Possible difference categories include:

- omission;
- altered dose;
- altered frequency;
- duplication;
- medication added or discontinued;
- formulary substitution;
- other medication changes.

An Indian discharge study involving 255 patients identified **412 discrepancies**, of which **191 were unintentional**; drug omission and altered dose were major categories.

```text
DIFFERENCE DETECTED
      ↓
IDENTIFY MEDICATION
      ↓
COMPARE SOURCES
      ↓
CHECK CLINICAL CONTEXT
      ↓

"Was this change INTENTIONAL?"
      ↓
```
